title: There’s a New Sea Spider in Town - Nautilus
gist: University of British Columbia researchers describe seven sea spider species from the Salish Sea in Organisms Diversity & Evolution, including two new species — the first new sea spiders found in the region in a century.

themes.theme: New Salish Sea sea spider species

insights.claim: University of British Columbia researchers described seven sea spider species from the Salish Sea in the journal Organisms Diversity & Evolution, five already known and two new to science.
insights.speaker: Devin Reese
insights.so_what: Low investment relevance; signals continued under-sampling of coastal Pacific Northwest marine biodiversity.

insights.claim: The two new Salish Sea sea spider species are the first new sea spiders discovered in that region in a century.
insights.speaker: Devin Reese
insights.so_what: Shows even well-studied coastal waters still yield new taxa — relevant context for marine biodiversity surveys and conservation policy.

insights.claim: Sea spiders are ancient arachnids closely related to scorpions, spiders and horseshoe crabs, sharing exoskeletons, jointed legs and chelicerae-type mouthparts for piercing or grabbing prey.
insights.speaker: Devin Reese
insights.so_what: Background science; no direct market signal.
insights.locator: As ancient arachnids closely related to scorpions

insights.claim: Sea spiders are unusual in having up to 12 legs, breathing through their skin and spawning eggs from their legs, traits honed over 500 million years of ocean life.
insights.speaker: Devin Reese
insights.so_what: Background science; no direct market signal.

insights.claim: Researchers describe the Salish Sea sea spiders as having hairy feet, legs dotted with eggs and tentacle-laden mouths likened to the Star Wars Sarlacc, a pop-culture framing used to publicize the taxonomy paper.
insights.speaker: Devin Reese
insights.so_what: Illustrates how niche taxonomy gets packaged for mass science media; no market signal.
